etymology: Hebrew Mikmas, a town of Benjamin east of Bethel, set among steep ravines; the scene of Jonathan's daring victory over the Philistine garrison.
biblical_def: Michmash was a town in the territory of Benjamin, perched among steep passes northeast of Jerusalem, famous as the scene of Jonathan's bold faith in 1 Samuel 14. The Philistines had gathered a vast host at Michmash, and Israel, disarmed and terrified, hid in caves and thickets. Then Jonathan, with only his armor-bearer, climbed on hands and feet up the crag between the rocks Bozez and Seneh, saying, "Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few" (1 Sam 14:6). The two of them killed some twenty men in a half-acre, and God sent a trembling through the whole Philistine camp; the earth quaked, the enemy turned their swords on one another, and Israel pursued them to a great victory. Michmash stands in the dictionary as the monument of Jonathan's faith, a perpetual witness that the LORD is not bound by numbers or weapons, and that He delights to save through the few who trust Him wholly when the many have lost heart.
webster_summary: A town of Benjamin among steep passes (1 Sam 14), where Jonathan and his armor-bearer routed the Philistine garrison in the faith that the LORD can save by many or by few; a monument to bold trust against overwhelming odds.

Where Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed the crag to the enemy garrison.
"There is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few" (1 Sam 14:6).
The LORD sent panic through the Philistine camp and gave Israel the victory.
scriptures: And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.

And the Philistines gathered themselves together to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots, and six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the sea shore in multitude: and they came up, and pitched in Michmash, eastward from Bethaven.
And there was trembling in the host, in the field, and among all the people: the garrison, and the spoilers, they also trembled, and the earth quaked: so it was a very great trembling.
So the LORD saved Israel that day: and the battle passed over unto Bethaven.
corruption_summary: Michmash needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God saves by His own power through the faith of the few, against every reliance on numbers, weapons, or human strength.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers-trusting misreading. The world measures the odds and counts the swords, as terrified Israel did at Michmash. Jonathan reckoned differently: the LORD is under no constraint of numbers, and can save by two as easily as by thousands. The dictionary holds that the battles of God are not decided by human resources; faith looks past the visible host to the invisible Lord, who delights to work when His people are weakest, that the glory may be plainly His.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is venturing faith. Jonathan did not presume; he said, "it may be that the LORD will work for us," and acted in humble boldness on the character of God. The dictionary commends his example: faith does not wait for guarantees but ventures on the power and goodness of the LORD, climbing the crag in the confidence that nothing restrains Him from saving.
roots_summary: A town of Benjamin among steep passes (1 Sam 14), where Jonathan and his armor-bearer routed the Philistine garrison in the faith that the LORD can save by many or by few.

etymology: Hebrew Geba, "hill," a Levitical town of Benjamin near the northern border of Judah, often paired with the phrase "from Geba to Beersheba."
biblical_def: Geba was a town of Benjamin assigned to the Levites (Josh 21:17), lying on the frontier between the northern and southern kingdoms and serving as a marker of Judah's northern boundary, as Beersheba marked the south: King Josiah's reforms reached "from Geba to Beersheba" (2 Kings 23:8). It was at Geba (closely tied to neighboring Gibeah) that Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison, the act that provoked the great gathering of the Philistines at Michmash (1 Sam 13:3). Later, King Asa of Judah fortified Geba with the stones of Ramah that Baasha had used against him, making it a defensive outpost of the kingdom (1 Kings 15:22). Geba reappears among the towns resettled by the returning exiles (Neh 11:31). Though never a great city, Geba's recurring mention as a border-marker and a fortified post makes it a quiet witness to the shape of the land God gave His people and the limits within which His covenant nation lived. It stands in the dictionary as a Levitical and frontier town, a reminder that the LORD apportioned to Israel a real inheritance with real boundaries, and set His ministers among the tribes throughout the land.
webster_summary: A Levitical town of Benjamin on Judah's northern frontier (Josh 21:17), the marker in the phrase "from Geba to Beersheba" (2 Kings 23:8); where Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison and which Asa later fortified.

corruption_summary: Geba needs no defense from redefinition; its recurring mention testifies to the concreteness of Israel's God-given inheritance and the LORD's provision of His ministers throughout the land.
corruption_paragraphs: Spiritualizing misreading. A vague, dehistoricized faith treats Israel's land and boundaries as mere symbol. Geba, named as a real border-town and a Levitical city, anchors the covenant in geography: God gave His people an actual inheritance with measured limits, and placed His Levites among every tribe to teach the law. The dictionary holds the historical reality of the inheritance as the ground of its typology; the heavenly hope rests on God's faithfulness in the earthly gift.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD's care to place His ministers among His people. Geba was a town set apart for the Levites, that the worship and instruction of God might be present throughout the land. The dictionary notes the pattern: God does not leave His people without teachers, but distributes the ministry of His Word among them, that none might be far from the knowledge of His ways.
roots_summary: A Levitical town of Benjamin on Judah's northern frontier (Josh 21:17), the marker in "from Geba to Beersheba"; where Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison and Asa fortified.

etymology: Hebrew Anathoth, a Levitical priestly town of Benjamin near Jerusalem; the home of the prophet Jeremiah and the place of Abiathar's banishment.
biblical_def: Anathoth was a priestly town of Benjamin, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem, given to the Levites as a city of refuge and dwelling (Josh 21:18). It is bound up with two notable men. First, to Anathoth King Solomon banished the priest Abiathar, sparing his life for the ark's sake but thrusting him from the priesthood, and so fulfilling the LORD's word against the house of Eli (1 Kings 2:26-27). Second, and most famously, Anathoth was the birthplace and home of Jeremiah, "of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin" (Jer 1:1). The prophet met bitter hostility from his own townsmen, who plotted against his life and forbade him to prophesy (Jer 11:21-23); yet it was at Anathoth that God commanded him to buy the field of his cousin Hanameel, even as the Babylonians besieged the land, as a sign that "houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land" (Jer 32:6-15). Anathoth stands in the dictionary as the prophet's home that turned against him, and as the place of a purchased field of hope — a double witness that the servant of God is often rejected by his own, yet that the LORD's promises of restoration are sure even in the hour of judgment.
webster_summary: A priestly town of Benjamin near Jerusalem (Josh 21:18), the home of Jeremiah and the place of Abiathar's banishment; where Jeremiah's own townsmen plotted against him, yet where he bought a field of hope amid the siege (Jer 32).

corruption_summary: Anathoth needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the rejection of the prophet by his own and the certainty of God's promises of restoration even under judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Honor-at-home misreading. The world expects the prophet to be most honored where he is best known. Anathoth shows the opposite: Jeremiah's own townsmen, his kin and neighbors, sought his life and silenced his word, a foreshadowing of Him who came to His own and was not received (John 1:11). The dictionary holds the sober pattern: faithfulness to God's word often costs the servant the favor of his own people, and the messenger must not measure truth by the welcome it receives at home.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is hope grounded in God's promise. At the darkest hour, with the Babylonians at the walls, God told Jeremiah to buy a field at Anathoth as a pledge that the land would yet be redeemed. The dictionary commends the act of faith: the believer, even in the midst of judgment and loss, may stake his confidence on the sure word of God, who promises restoration beyond the ruin.
roots_summary: A priestly town of Benjamin near Jerusalem (Josh 21:18), the home of Jeremiah and the place of Abiathar's banishment; where the prophet bought a field of hope amid the siege.

etymology: Hebrew Gibon, a major town of the Hivites north of Jerusalem; the home of the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua, and the great high place where the tabernacle stood and Solomon sought wisdom.
biblical_def: Gibeon was a notable city north of Jerusalem, prominent in Israel's history at several turns. Its inhabitants, the Gibeonites, fearing destruction, deceived Joshua and the elders with worn clothes and mouldy bread into making a league of peace; when the ruse was discovered, Israel kept its oath but made them "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the house of God (Josh 9). When five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon for this league, Joshua came to its defense, and the LORD cast down great hailstones and made the sun stand still over Gibeon until Israel was avenged (Josh 10:11-13). At the pool of Gibeon, Abner's and Joab's men fought their deadly contest (2 Sam 2:12-17), and there Joab later murdered Amasa (2 Sam 20:8-10). After the ark was moved, the tabernacle of the LORD and the brazen altar remained at Gibeon, "the great high place," and there Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings; the LORD appeared to him by night and gave him the wise and understanding heart he asked for above riches and long life (1 Kings 3:4-12; 2 Chr 1:3-12). Gibeon stands in the dictionary as the city of the kept oath, the standing sun, and the gift of wisdom — a place where God honored Israel's faithfulness to its word and answered the prayer for understanding.
webster_summary: A major town north of Jerusalem (Josh 9-10): home of the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua into a league Israel honored, the place where the sun stood still, and the great high place where Solomon offered sacrifice and received his wise and understanding heart (1 Kings 3).

corruption_summary: Gibeon is corrupted when the sun standing still is dismissed as myth, or when the binding force of Israel's oath to the Gibeonites is treated as primitive scruple rather than the seriousness of a vow before God.
corruption_paragraphs: Miracle-denied misreading. Naturalism explains away the long day at Gibeon as legend or poetic exaggeration. Scripture records it as a real act of the God who rules the heavens, answering Joshua's bold prayer. The dictionary holds the miracle as written: the Maker of the sun is free to govern it as He wills, and the God who parted the sea and raised the dead is not constrained by the ordinary course He Himself ordained. To strip Gibeon of its wonder is to deny the Lord of creation.

Oath-trivialized misreading. Modern readers often think Israel foolish to keep a league won by deception. Scripture treats the sworn oath as sacred: because the princes had sworn by the LORD, the covenant stood, and centuries later God sent famine on the land for Saul's breach of it (2 Sam 21:1-2). The dictionary recovers the weight of a vow before God: an oath in His name binds the conscience, and faithfulness to one's word, even when costly, honors the God who is Himself faithful.
roots_summary: A major town north of Jerusalem (Josh 9-10): home of the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua, the place of the standing sun, and the great high place where Solomon received wisdom (1 Kings 3).

etymology: Hebrew Yabesh Gilad, a town of Gilead east of the Jordan; bound to Saul by gratitude and to David by an act of loyal courage.
biblical_def: Jabesh-gilead was a town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, whose history is woven through with rescue and gratitude. When Nahash the Ammonite besieged it and demanded the right eye of every man as the price of surrender, the threatened city sent for help, and Saul, newly anointed, was moved by the Spirit of God to muster Israel and deliver them in a great victory — the deed that confirmed his kingship (1 Sam 11). The men of Jabesh-gilead never forgot it. Years later, when the Philistines slew Saul and his sons and fastened their bodies to the wall of Beth-shan, the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead arose, traveled all night, took down the bodies, and gave them honorable burial under a tree, with seven days' fasting (1 Sam 31:11-13). David blessed them for this kindness to their fallen king (2 Sam 2:4-6). The town appears earlier too, in the tragic aftermath of the Benjamite war (Judg 21). Jabesh-gilead stands in the dictionary as the city of remembered deliverance and grateful loyalty, a witness that kindness received should be kindness returned, and that honor shown to the dead and the fallen is a mark of a faithful and noble heart.
webster_summary: A town of Gilead east of the Jordan (1 Sam 11; 31), delivered by Saul from Nahash the Ammonite; in grateful loyalty its valiant men later recovered Saul's body from the wall of Beth-shan and buried him with honor.

corruption_summary: Jabesh-gilead needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is grateful loyalty — that deliverance received obliges kindness returned, and that honoring the fallen is a mark of a noble and faithful heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Ingratitude-excusing misreading. A self-centered age forgets its benefactors and counts loyalty optional. The men of Jabesh-gilead remembered, across many years, the king who had saved them, and risked their lives by night to honor his dishonored body. The dictionary holds that gratitude is a binding virtue: kindness received lays a real obligation of kindness returned, and the faithful heart does not forget the hand that delivered it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is honor toward the dead and the fallen. The valiant men of Jabesh did a hard and dangerous deed for one who could no longer reward them, simply because it was right. The dictionary commends such loyalty: to honor those who have died, to give the fallen a decent burial, to show kindness that cannot be repaid, is a reflection of the steadfast love of God Himself.
roots_summary: A town of Gilead east of the Jordan (1 Sam 11; 31), delivered by Saul from Nahash; in grateful loyalty its valiant men later recovered and buried Saul's body with honor.

etymology: Hebrew Apheq, "fortress" or "stronghold"; the name of several towns, chiefly the Philistine staging-place where Israel lost the ark, and the site of Israel's victory over Syria.
biblical_def: Aphek was the name of more than one town in Scripture, two of them notable. At an Aphek on the coastal plain the Philistines pitched their camp before the disastrous battle in which Israel, presuming on the ark of God as a talisman, carried it into battle without repentance and saw it captured, Eli's sons slain, and the glory departed from Israel (1 Sam 4:1-11). The lesson burned deep: the symbols of God's presence avail nothing where the heart is far from Him. At another Aphek, east of the Sea of Galilee, the Syrians under Ben-hadad regrouped after their defeat, boasting that the LORD was a god of the hills and not of the valleys; God gave them into Israel's hand to teach them "that I am the LORD" (1 Kings 20:26-30). It was likewise at Aphek that the Philistines mustered before the battle of Gilboa, where Saul fell (1 Sam 29:1). Aphek stands in the dictionary as a place of solemn instruction: that God will not be used as a charm by an unrepentant people, and that He vindicates His own name against every boast that would confine His power, proving Himself the LORD of the valleys as of the hills.
webster_summary: A town (or towns) named "stronghold": the Philistine camp where Israel presumptuously lost the ark (1 Sam 4), and the place where God defeated the Syrians who called Him a god of the hills only (1 Kings 20); a witness that God is not a talisman and not confined.

Where God defeated the Syrians who said He was a god of the hills only (1 Kings 20:26-30).

1 Kings 20:28

1 Kings 20:30

corruption_summary: Aphek is corrupted when its lessons are missed: that sacred symbols cannot substitute for a repentant heart, and that the living God will not be confined to any sphere or boast.
corruption_paragraphs: Talisman-religion misreading. At Aphek Israel treated the ark as a magic charm that would guarantee victory regardless of their sin, and lost both the battle and the ark. The same error lives wherever men trust in religious objects, rituals, or affiliations while their hearts remain unrepentant. The dictionary holds the searching lesson: the presence of God is no talisman; He will not be used by a rebellious people, and the outward symbols of religion avail nothing apart from true faith and obedience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unconfined sovereignty of God. The Syrians imagined they could escape the LORD by fighting in the valleys; He proved Himself God of valley and hill alike. The dictionary commends the truth Aphek teaches: no boast, no terrain, no power can limit the living God, who vindicates His name against all who would shrink Him to a tribal or local deity, that all may know He is the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Shunem, a town of Issachar in the Jezreel valley; the home of the hospitable woman who lodged Elisha and whose son he raised from the dead.
biblical_def: Shunem was a town of Issachar in the valley of Jezreel, remembered chiefly for the great-hearted woman whose story fills 2 Kings 4. Perceiving that Elisha was a holy man of God who passed her way, she and her husband built and furnished a little chamber on the wall, that the prophet might lodge there. For her kindness Elisha promised, against all hope, that she would bear a son, and so it came to pass. When the boy, grown, died suddenly of a stroke in the harvest field, she laid him on the prophet's bed, rode hard to Carmel, clung to Elisha's feet, and would not be turned aside; the prophet came, prayed, stretched himself upon the child, and God restored him to life (2 Kings 4:8-37). Years later Elisha's word saved her from famine and recovered her land (2 Kings 8:1-6). Shunem was also where the Philistines encamped before the battle of Gilboa (1 Sam 28:4), and the home of Abishag, who cherished the aged David (1 Kings 1:3). Shunem stands in the dictionary as the town of the Shunammite woman, a lasting picture of hospitality to God's servants and of faith that holds fast to God in the face of death, rewarded by the God who gives and restores life.
webster_summary: A town of Issachar in the Jezreel valley (2 Kings 4), home of the hospitable Shunammite woman who lodged Elisha; God gave her a son and, when he died, raised him through the prophet — a picture of hospitality and persevering faith.

Where, when the child died, Elisha raised him to life (2 Kings 4:32-37).

corruption_paragraphs: Hospitality-diminished misreading. A transactional age sees little value in opening one's home to a passing servant of God. The Shunammite built a room for the prophet expecting nothing, and God rewarded her beyond her asking. The dictionary holds the biblical honor of hospitality: to receive a prophet in the name of a prophet is to receive a prophet's reward (Matt 10:41), and kindness to God's servants is kindness the LORD Himself remembers and repays.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faith that holds fast in grief. When her son lay dead, the Shunammite did not despair but rode straight to the man of God, and to every anxious question answered, "It is well." The dictionary commends her persevering trust: faith in the hour of loss does not deny the pain but clings to the God of life, and Shunem became the place where the God who gives also proved Himself the God who raises the dead.
roots_summary: A town of Issachar in the Jezreel valley (2 Kings 4), home of the hospitable Shunammite woman who lodged Elisha; God gave her a son and raised him from death through the prophet.

Is it well with the child? And she answered, It is well (2 Kings 4:26).
Shunem pictures hospitality to God's servants and faith that holds fast in the face of death.

etymology: Hebrew Timnah, a town on the border of Judah and Dan in Philistine country; the scene of Samson's ill-matched marriage and of Judah's encounter with Tamar.
biblical_def: Timnah was a town on the borderland between Judah, Dan, and Philistia, the setting of two sobering narratives. There Samson saw a Philistine woman and demanded of his parents, "get her for me; for she pleaseth me well," against their plea that he take a wife from his own people (Judg 14:1-3). On the way to Timnah he tore a lion as one tears a kid, and from its carcass came the riddle of honey; but the marriage, contracted with an unbelieving people, ended in betrayal, bloodshed, and the unraveling of his calling. The episode is a standing warning against being unequally yoked, against marrying for the eyes rather than the fear of God. Timnath was also the place to which Judah went up to his sheepshearers, where his daughter-in-law Tamar, wronged and denied her right, met him in disguise (Gen 38:12-14) — a tangled account of sin and providence in the line that would nonetheless lead to Christ. Timnah stands in the dictionary as a place of warning: that the desires of the eyes, indulged against the counsel of God, bring sorrow, and that even into such broken stories the LORD weaves His sovereign and redemptive purpose.
webster_summary: A town on the Judah-Dan-Philistine border: the place of Samson's ill-matched marriage to a Philistine woman against his parents' counsel (Judg 14), and of Judah's encounter with Tamar (Gen 38); a warning against the unequal yoke and the lust of the eyes.

On the road to which he tore a lion, source of the later riddle.
Where the unequal marriage ended in betrayal and bloodshed.
Also where Judah met Tamar at the sheepshearing (Gen 38:12-14).
scriptures: Judg 14:2
And he came up, and told his father and his mother, and said, I have seen a woman in Timnath of the daughters of the Philistines: now therefore get her for me to wife.
Judg 14:3

Then his father and his mother said unto him, Is there never a woman among the daughters of thy brethren, or among all my people, that thou goest to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines? And Samson said unto his father, Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well.
And it was told Tamar, saying, Behold thy father in law goeth up to Timnath to shear his sheep.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
corruption_summary: Timnah is corrupted when Samson's demand is romanticized as following one's heart, rather than read as the warning Scripture intends against the unequal yoke and the rule of the eyes over the fear of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Follow-your-heart misreading. The world celebrates Samson's "she pleaseth me well" as the triumph of love over restriction. Scripture frames it as the first step in his ruin: a marriage to an unbelieving people, chosen by the eyes against the counsel of his godly parents and the law of God. The dictionary holds the warning plainly: desire that overrides the fear of God and the wisdom of counsel leads to sorrow, and the heart is not a safe guide when it is set against the Word.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition beyond this. The principle to recover is the danger of the unequal yoke. Believers are not to bind themselves in covenant intimacy with those who reject the Lord (2 Cor 6:14). Yet Timnah teaches a second truth as well: even through the broken and sinful (Samson's folly, Judah's shame), God works His sovereign purpose, weaving redemption through the tangled threads of human failure, for from Judah's line came the Christ.
roots_summary: A town on the Judah-Dan-Philistine border: the place of Samson's ill-matched Philistine marriage (Judg 14) and of Judah's encounter with Tamar (Gen 38); a warning against the unequal yoke.

etymology: Hebrew Sokoh, a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah; the staging-ground of the Philistines before the combat of David and Goliath.
biblical_def: Socoh was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, best known as the place where the Philistines gathered their armies for the confrontation that brought David and Goliath face to face. "Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which belongeth to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim" (1 Sam 17:1). There, in the valley of Elah between the two camps, the giant of Gath defied the armies of the living God morning and evening for forty days, until a shepherd boy came with his sling and five smooth stones, declaring, "the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands" (1 Sam 17:47). Socoh thus forms the backdrop of one of Scripture's greatest displays of faith over fear, of the LORD's power magnified through the weak and despised. The town appears also among the cities of Judah and as one of Solomon's commissary districts. Socoh stands in the dictionary as the place where the hosts of the uncircumcised mustered against Israel, and where God answered their champion's boast not with a greater giant but with a boy who trusted in the name of the LORD of hosts.
webster_summary: A town in the Judean lowland (1 Sam 17:1) where the Philistines mustered before the battle of David and Goliath in the nearby valley of Elah; the backdrop of faith's victory over the giant in the name of the LORD of hosts.

corruption_summary: Socoh needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the battle is the LORD's, won not by sword and spear but by faith in the name of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_paragraphs: Strength-trusting misreading. The Philistines at Socoh trusted in their giant, their armor, and their weapons; Israel trembled at the same. David reckoned by faith: the battle belongs to the LORD, who saves not with sword and spear. The dictionary holds the abiding lesson: the contests of God's people are not decided by visible might, and the believer who comes in the name of the LORD of hosts has on his side a power the strongest enemy cannot match.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is zeal for the honor of God's name. David's indignation rose not at personal insult but because the giant "defied the armies of the living God." The dictionary commends his motive: faith is moved most by the dishonor done to God, and acts for the vindication of His name. At Socoh the boast of the flesh fell before the boy who cared more for the glory of the LORD than for his own safety.
roots_summary: A town in the Judean lowland (1 Sam 17:1) where the Philistines mustered before David and Goliath met in the valley of Elah; the backdrop of faith's victory over the giant.

etymology: Hebrew Gibah, "hill"; a town of Benjamin, the home and royal seat of King Saul, and earlier the scene of a terrible crime against a Levite's concubine.
biblical_def: Gibeah was a town of Benjamin, set on a hill north of Jerusalem, remembered both as the home and capital of King Saul and as the site of one of the darkest episodes in the book of Judges. In the days when there was no king in Israel, a Levite's concubine was abused to death by the wicked men of Gibeah, an outrage so great that it provoked civil war and the near-extinction of the tribe of Benjamin (Judg 19-20). The prophets long after invoked "the days of Gibeah" as a byword for depravity (Hos 9:9; 10:9). Yet Gibeah was also the home of Saul, son of Kish, and became his royal residence after he was made king; there he gathered the men whose hearts God had touched (1 Sam 10:26), and from there he reigned (1 Sam 11:4; 15:34). The contrast is sobering: the town of Israel's first king carried in its memory the worst of the lawless age that cried out for a king. Gibeah stands in the dictionary as a double witness — to the depths of human depravity when every man does what is right in his own eyes, and to the rise of the monarchy that God granted His people, with all its promise and its peril.
webster_summary: A town of Benjamin (Judg 19-20; 1 Sam 10): the home and royal seat of King Saul, and earlier the scene of the atrocity against a Levite's concubine that became a byword for depravity; a double witness to lawless sin and to the rise of the monarchy.

corruption_summary: Gibeah is corrupted when the horror of Judges 19 is excused or relativized; its memory stands as a witness against the lie that human beings left to themselves drift toward goodness rather than depravity.
corruption_paragraphs: Human-goodness misreading. The optimistic creed of the age insists that people, freed from constraint, tend toward decency. Gibeah testifies otherwise: when there was no king and every man did what was right in his own eyes, a whole town descended to an atrocity that sickened the nation. The dictionary holds the biblical doctrine of human depravity against every sentimental denial: the heart unrestrained is not safe but savage, and the days of Gibeah show what man becomes when the fear of God is cast off.

This entry faces little further postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the necessity of righteous authority. The recurring lament of Judges — "in those days there was no king in Israel" — frames Gibeah as the fruit of lawlessness, and points forward to the longing for a righteous ruler. The dictionary notes the trajectory: even flawed Saul's monarchy was God's answer to anarchy, and the whole story strains toward the true and righteous King, the Son of David, whose reign alone heals what Gibeah revealed.
